title: Shirudo: OpenAI and Cisco's open-source runtime for shielding unpatched Linux
author: acossta

title: Re: Shirudo: OpenAI and Cisco's open-source runtime fo...
text:
I like the idea, but am not sure they've nailed an acceptable (to me) implementation. I'll be the first to admit I don't fully understand it, so maybe someone here can enlighten me.

I gather the eBPF bits run local (and can even be set up to deploy out of a repository you host).

But to get most effective use out of this tech, it seems like you'd need to give an AI vendor (namely OpenAI) a bunch of telemetry and more potential control into your systems than I'm sure I'd be comfortable with. I take it AI will be writing code that gets injected directly inside your kernel. By nature of being eBPF, Linux offers protections and sandboxing, but I wouldn't put it past the tools to find an exploit (or some kind of sidechannel utilizing an in-kernal eBPF and usermode malware). Feels like a tempting target for bad actors to try and compromise to get a foothold into systems.

At the end of the day, I'm not sure I'd personally trust OpenAI (or Cisco for that matter) for this sort of application. I'm inclined to wait until a company with some more security pedigree comes out with something I perceive as more trustworthy (I appreciate the open-source aspect and see potential for others to join and build on the work). And from a practical standpoint, their model of mitigation delivery seems more meant to help companies that have fleets of servers for which they're struggling to keep pace on update deployments, than those who already have a tight deployment cycle in place. I do see how AI agents could identify threats and come up with mitigations faster than any human counterpart (though am wondering how many false positives we'll see in practice, or breaking of behavior that isn't actually part of an attack). You either trust the AI to get the mitigations right, or are back to waiting for human-reviewed versions.

Again, I'm by no means an expert, and would love to know what the experts think.
author: rkagerer

title: Re: Shirudo: OpenAI and Cisco's open-source runtime fo...
text:
It sounds like a cool idea, at least the way OpenAI presents it.

However, going to the page and requirements, I have to nope out. This basically requires a full measured boot setup (TPM2, unified kernel image etc.).

This is definitely not a simple "vibe-code your patch" platform you can deploy in an emergency.

I wish there was a reduced security mode that really just focuses on patching vulnerable software, and not defending itself from when the machine is already compromised as root.

Because if your organization already has this bleeding-edge measured boot setup, then I believe quickly deploying a patch really is not a big deal anymore.

title: Show HN: Claudia – focused manager for Claude CLI settings.json
text:
Long story short, I needed a way to enable/disable skills for specific projects, but for how nice Claude CLI is, it kinda sucks in this regard.

I wanted it to do 2-3 things well, be fast, and not bloat it. Of course, I then prompted it into existence.

Features: - Shows the available settings for your specific Claude version (always in sync). - Configure CLAUDE.md, settings.json, Skills, Plugins and MCPs. - Tree-view in the sidebar to view all Claude projects. - Gives useful suggestions for enabling privacy-related settings.

It's a single Go binary for macOS, Linux and Windows, MIT licensed.

You can find a screenshot and more info here: https://github.com/claude-settings-xyz/claudia

Curious what you think (and how it's so bad and vibecoded).

---

If you like such tools, these 2 might be helpful: - CODEXED — The same thing but for Codex CLI (https://github.com/codex-config/codexed) - SWITCHEROO — Switch local CLI accounts for 10+ providers (Wrangler, Vercel, Claude, Github etc) (https://github.com/FTCHD/switcheroo)

title: Re: Show HN: Trieste – A desktop app to organize work ...
text:
Hi! I'm a solo French developer. Over the past few years, I've been trying to change the way I code with AI, and I was fairly dissatisfied with how work was organized in the standard tools, which I found suboptimal and mentally exhausting. So I built my own interface, which I'm now making available to the public. I believe it offers an original approach. I'll let you be the judge.

The core idea: common tools usually offer monolithic, disposable conversations with coding agents. When one fills up or you close it, you have to re-explain everything to the next one, or put together complicated, fragile Markdown docs (automatic compaction slowly destroys the context... it's the same problem). So I wanted to tie each agent to a persistent context, which I call a "nest".

Technically, a nest is just a folder of Markdown files in your project, with a required structure and a few generic instructions automatically injected into the context of the agent in charge of it. The agent keeps the docs, pending decisions, the plan, etc. up to date there; after the conversation is compacted or regenerated, the next agent picks up the work by loading only the relevant context.

Each nest is represented by an avatar on a canvas, and the nests can communicate with each other. The result is like a small company coming to life before your eyes, which lets you follow the work.

The app plugs into the official CLIs of Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Antigravity, on macOS, Windows and Linux. It's paid (one-time purchase, closed source), with a full 30-day trial, no account required.

Demo (2 min 37 s): https://youtu.be/ItkgQVCnxNI

Feel free to visit my website, where I say a bit more about it. The tool is already quite polished, but not yet battle-tested: only four of us are using it so far.

Thanks for reading. All feedback is welcome.
